records.text: One piece, two victims. This is a fork: a single piece goes after several targets, and one move may not be enough to save them all.
Simple problem: this lets one of their pieces fork several targets. Before moving, look for the square where that piece could land.
Simple point: a fork was sitting right here, with one piece able to hit several targets, and the move played walks past it.
The main thing is the pin. That piece has its own king behind it on that line, so it cannot leave the line, and it stays stuck.
Simple problem: a pin against the king is now on offer for the other side, and a piece caught in it stays stuck in place.
A pin against the king was the better move, because it would have nailed a piece to its line. Here that piece gets to move freely.
Big idea: a skewer. The front piece is hit, it has to get out of the way, and the piece behind it is left to be taken.
Two pieces are lined up on one line, and now a skewer is on for the other side. When the front piece shifts off, the back piece is a target.
A skewer was the better move: the front piece is hit, it steps away, and the one behind is left to be taken. So that chance is gone.
The guard goes first. This move hits the defender, and whatever it was holding up is left with no help.
One defender is holding things together, and now the other side gets to knock it out. Look at what that defender holds up before it is gone.
The better move went after the defender. Without it, the piece it guarded would have stood with no help. As played, that defender is still standing guard.
Plain fact: its own pieces leave the king no air on the back row, and this move goes straight for it. That is mate on the back row in the making.
Simple problem: the king has no air. Its own pieces box it in on the back row, and the other side can aim for mate there.
The king was boxed in on its back row by its own pieces, so a back-rank mate was ready to go. The move played does something else.
The big thing is the pawn. It is walking toward the last row, where it gets promoted, so follow that walk.
One of their pawns now has a clear walk toward the last row, and if it gets there it is promoted. That pawn needs watching.
The better move cleared a pawn's walk to the last row and a promotion. The move played leaves that pawn sitting still.
The front piece clears out and a hidden attacker behind it comes alive. Big idea: a discovered attack, where moving one piece wakes up another.
Their front piece is standing in the way of a piece behind it, and this move lets it step aside so the back one can attack. Discovered attacks begin exactly like this.
There was a discovered attack in the better move. Clear the blocker away, and the back piece attacks as well. Not played here.
A single move, aimed at two things. That is a double attack, and the defense has to deal with both of them.
With this, the other side gets a double attack. Any reply has to cover both targets.
Two at once: that is what the better move hit. A double attack was there, and the move played makes no such threat.
This move drags a defender off its post, so whatever it was guarding has no cover now. Plain deflection.
A single defender carries a lot here, and the other side can now drag it away and leave that work undone. Deflection is the name for that.
Dragging a defender off its post was the better move. That chance to deflect it is left on the board.
Simple point: it was loose, and this move takes it.
The better move takes a piece with no guard on it. The move played leaves it sitting there. Loose pieces come first.
Simple problem: one piece has nobody guarding it, so the other side gets it for nothing.
Simple problem: this moves the only real defender away from a piece. That piece can now be collected.
With its last move, the opponent made a threat, and this move does nothing about it; a piece hangs because of it. The other side's move always gets looked at first.
This capture starts a bad trade. The recapture takes back a bigger piece. Count a trade all the way to its last capture.
Bottom line: a minor piece is out of its starting spot and ready to work.
Development was there with a different move.
Big plus for the rook: the file it stands on has no pawns of either color, so it has a clear road.
A different move would have put a rook on a file empty of pawns.
Half-open file: that is where this rook now stands. Its own pawns are off that file, and an enemy pawn is still sitting there in front of it.
A different move would have set a rook on a half-open file, its own pawns gone and an enemy pawn still there to aim at.
Big thing: a passed pawn. No enemy pawn waits ahead to stop it, on its own file or either side file.
Another move would have turned a pawn into a passer, its own file and both side files clear of enemy pawns ahead.
Up goes the passed pawn, a row closer to promotion. It was free already; now it has less distance left.
With a different move, the passer would have gone up one more row.
Big picture: no friendly pawn is near this one any more. With no friendly pawn on the files beside it, no pawn can help guard it.
A different move would have left a pawn standing by itself with no friendly pawn next door on either side.
Simple point: a loose piece now has protection. It is not hanging any more.
A different move would have given cover to a loose piece.
Plain fact: this piece has lost its guard. Weak spot, yes; lost piece, no.
Another move would have taken the last guard away from a piece. A loose piece is a target, not a lost piece.
Simple point: the king gets elbow room, one more legal square. Good to have that room.
A different move would have given the king more breathing room.
Castling: the king tucks away to the side, and the rook comes over next to it, all in a single move.
Castling was there instead, king tucked away and rook brought out on the same move.
After this capture, that side's two bishops are not a pair any more. That side is left without one bishop for the light squares and one for the dark.
With a different move, a bishop capture would have broken up the opponent's pair.
Bottom line: doubled pawns. That side has two pawns on a single file now, stacked up, and neither can guard the other.
Doubled pawns would have come from a different move, two pawns of one color stacked up.
This is the big problem: from this point, mate by force belongs to the other side. Track back to where the defense broke.
Big picture: mate by force was there, and the move played skips it. When the king is trapped, look at every check first.
Material goes, and the idea holds. If the material is grabbed, the checked line still works. That is strong.
Simple point: every other checked move lost. This was the one move left standing. Good defense.
Plain fact: no other checked move kept the edge. With anything else, the advantage was gone.
Simple problem: something is loose, and the reply takes it at once. Look at the reply and find the loose piece.
Check is the best answer. When the king is attacked, that is the first thing to deal with.
The engine has a different move on top. Play that one as well, then see how the replies differ.
The engine has a better move than this one. The cost shows up in the reply.
Strong. Out of everything the engine weighed, this move gives up next to nothing.
This is sound. The engine likes another move more, but the value of the position mostly stays.
Natural, says the human-move model. It still is not the best one. A stronger move is on the engine's list.
This move surprises the human-move model. Even so, the engine has it as strong. Rare does not mean wrong.
There was exactly one move that kept the position playable, and it was missed. The human-move model says that one was hard to come up with. Learn it anyway.
Hard to find, by the human-move model, and the other moves that were checked back that up. Keep this one in your memory.
Without this move, the position falls. The human-move model and the other checked moves say it was a hard defense to find. Well held.
The human-move model calls this natural, and it is also the engine's best move. The easy choice and the right choice are the same.
The human-move model has this down as natural. The engine calls it strong, though it likes one move a little more.
Next to nothing left on the clock for this one. Little time makes every move harder.
Played fast, while there was still time on the clock.
This move cost a lot of thinking time. That is fine when it finds something.
Simple point: this one is straight out of opening theory. A known line is one thing. Understanding the position is another.
This is the move where known opening theory runs out. From now on, the players are working it out for themselves.
The earlier setback is fixed; this move gets the game back on track. Good. Keep building from here.
Some of the other side's mistakes helped, and the game is playable again after the earlier setback. Take that, but do not count on it.
The opponent made a slip on the last move, and this move cashes in. Good.
The opponent just blundered, and nobody makes them pay here. When they slip, look for the punishment.
Bottom line: this game has run into the same problem once already. Lay the two moments next to each other and find the common thread.
Big picture: the earlier loose piece is safe behind a guard now. Good.
Not one big mistake. A few small slips have added up, and this move is one more of those.
The advantage was kept, move after move, until the game was won. That is how to finish.
Simple point: the saved games have this problem in them more than once. That makes it worth real study.
Checkmate. Nowhere left for that king to go. Finished.
Checkmate. That king has no move left. The defense broke earlier, so go back and find that spot.
A draw. The result is settled, but the moves are still worth a look.
Look at the board, then pick a move.
Not quite. Back to the board; a different move this time.
That try did not get checked. Go back to the move and play it again.
Saved engine analysis: the side that played this move has a forced mate in hand.
Saved engine analysis: after this move, mate is forced against the side that played it.
At the last move of the saved line, count the material. The side that played this move has more than it had at the start.
At the last move of the saved line, count the material. The side that played this move has less than it had at the start.
This exercise takes the move as correct. No clear tactical reason here, and no made-up one either.
Wrong answer for this exercise. There is no clear tactical reason in these moves either way.
Plain fact: the exercise lists this move among its saved answers. In this exercise, that list is the rule.
Simple point: the exercise did not save this move as an answer. It is not bad chess for that. This exercise simply wants something else.
Look at this move until it makes sense. Then move on.
Good move. Hold on to the why, too.
Practice saved, and the schedule for review is untouched.
Solved. This recall still stays on the relearning list for now.
Start here, with the position before any of the moves we look at.
Next move. See what changed.
Check. The king is under attack, and that comes before everything.
This move ends the check on the king.
Up to the last row, and the pawn is promoted.
Up to the last row, and the pawn is promoted with check.
Up to the last row, and the pawn is promoted. That is checkmate, and the king is trapped.
The pawn makes it to the last row and is promoted, and that same move gets its king out of check.
A capture.
Capture and check together. The piece takes, and the king is attacked.
Something is captured, and it is checkmate. The king cannot get away.
A capture, and the capture is what gets the king out of check.
One pawn move does it all: a capture, and a promotion on the last row.
The pawn captures as it reaches the last row, is promoted, and gives check.
One pawn move does it all: a capture, and a promotion on the last row. Checkmate follows, with the king trapped.
One pawn move does it all: a capture, and a promotion on the last row. That same move lifts the check on its king.
The king castles, and the rook gives check from its new square.
Castling ends the game with checkmate. The enemy king is caught with no way out.
Here the fork collects. One piece goes after several targets, takes one, and this example comes out ahead in material.
Pinned to its king, that piece may not make the capture shown, because stepping off the line would give the king away.
The attacked piece has its king behind it, so it is pinned. Its only moves are ones that still cover the king, so running is hard.
Not one defender may take back, because each of them is pinned to its king. That makes the capture work, and material is won in the line shown.
With its king behind it, the pinned piece is nailed to that line. As these moves go on, it gets taken.
Bottom line: once the front piece is gone from the line, whatever was behind it is captured.
Check. The king must move out of the way. Then the same attacker wins what was behind the king.
First the guard goes, and it was the only guard. The piece it was protecting falls later in these moves.
First the defender gets dragged away, then the piece it was protecting gets taken.
Front piece moves, the line clears, and the back piece makes a capture along it.
Move the front piece, and check comes from behind it.
Two checks land on the king in the same move: double check. Nothing but a king move will do against that.
One piece moves and attacks, and the line it leaves lets a second attacker in. Here, that second attacker takes what it was aiming at.
The pawn is promoted, and in this example that side ends the line with extra material.
That piece was loose, so it goes. This example ends with the capturing side holding extra material.
Big picture: the attacking piece was under a relative pin, and the opponent's last move freed it. The target did not move, so in the line shown it is taken.
Nothing in the rules stops the other side from playing that marked move. Try that reply on the board and judge what follows.
Before every move, find any piece of yours that could be taken for nothing.
Loose enemy pieces get checked before any quiet move.
Go through every forcing move hunting for a fork on two valuable targets.
Before moving a pinned piece, look past it down the line: the king may be there, or a bigger piece.
An attack can go straight through the first piece. Look for a valuable piece lined up behind it.
A defender about to be traded: see what it guards first.
A blocker that moves opens up whatever line is behind it. Follow it to the end.
Some moves carry two threats at once. Look hard for those. Checks and opened lines both count as threats.
A back-row defender leaving means the king may lose its air. Check for an escape square first.
Count the pawn's moves to promotion, and look at every forcing pawn push.
A defender about to move: first count what it guards. All of that loses its guard when it leaves.
A trade gets counted to the very end, every capture on both sides.
A forcing trade may drag a defender away from a second job it has. Watch for it.
This one is measured against the saved answers. Moves outside that list may still be fine chess.
The replies in these moves are strong ones. A strong reply is not always the only reply.
Only the line shown is counted for material, starting where it starts. Piece values for that count are in the written notes.
No single simple tactic explains the saved line. Run through it move by move and compare how the replies differ. No positional reason is assumed either.
The saved answer setting decides this explanation. Which one is set is in the written notes.
Here comes your study line, move by move.
Right. It belongs to the line you are learning.
The answer is somewhere in your picked study lines. One of those moves fits here.
Several moves from your picked opening lines are fine here. Any of them counts.
Only one move here comes from your study material. Find it.
Not in the opening lines you picked. Try again.
Not one of your picked opening moves. Try again. The study was changed, and its review dates stay where they are.
Not one of your picked opening moves. Try again. Because this position is retired, nothing about its schedule moves.
Any move in this line is good enough for mixed Due. Dedicated practice sticks to this single line.
The recall schedule tests the side you picked. One card covers a position that several active studies share.
Simple fix: the session has to be reloaded before the next move.
Here the board runs the checked line.
Answer shown, and this try is saved that way. Play it through below.
Second try, and solved. Both go on your record: the miss, then the finish.
Not one wrong move from start to finish. Good.
Not the puzzle's move. Moves played right before it are kept.
Right move. The puzzle is not done yet. Another move is waiting.
No rush. Think it through, then move.
Not enough from the engine on this one, so I have no explanation to give.
Review on pause. Start it again below, or push a piece around to look.
Pick a move to review it, or try a move of your own.
Simple point: book move.
Plain fact: this is a move theory has seen many times.
Book. Theory has written this one down.
Still book.
Book again for this one.
Both sides are still in theory with the reply.
Known line, still going.
More book.
The book again, one more time.
Still covered by the opening books.
Book again. Book does not mean good.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and it walks into a forced mate for the other side. Natural or not, go back and find where the defense broke.
Simple point: there was a forced mate to play. The human-move model calls the move played the natural pick, and the mate slips away. Every check gets looked at first.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, but the reply takes something at once. Natural is fine, but the reply still has to be answered.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick. The engine still finds something better, and some value goes. Easy-looking moves need checking too.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and now one of their pieces can fork several targets. Look for that square first.
By the human-move model, this is a natural pick. It also lines two pieces up for a skewer. When the front piece shifts off, the back piece is a target.
Bottom line: every other checked move lost, and this one held. The human-move model rates that defense difficult, and it was found anyway.
Every other checked move lost, and this was the move that kept the game in one piece. By the human-move model and the checked moves, a hard one to find. Strong.
Big picture: this move is the only reason the advantage lasted; every other checked move lost. The human-move model says that resource was hard to find. Found anyway.
The advantage hung on this move alone; every other checked move lost. The human-move model and the checked moves say it was a hard find. Strong.
Fork. A lone attacker, and a handful of targets. The human-move model rates it an unusual pick, and the engine marks it strong. Rare, and still right.
Fork, and the engine's first choice. One attacker, more than one target. The human-move model and the checked moves both point to a hard one to spot. Strong.
A pin, with the king behind. If it moves, its own king is open to attack, so it stays. The human-move model rates the move unusual; the engine puts it in the strong column.
The engine's top move pins a piece to its king, and that piece stays stuck on its line. By the human-move model, not easy to come up with. Strong.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick. It also moves the only real defender off a piece, and the other side can take that piece. Natural, and still a mistake.

Simple problem: the one real defender leaves, and what it covered is up for grabs. One checked move held instead, and the human-move model says it was a hard thing to see. That move goes on the study list.

The opponent's last move carried a threat to deal with. By the human-move model this reply is natural, but it leaves the threat standing, and a piece hangs. The other side's move gets looked at first.
After this move, the opponent's threat is still standing, and a piece hangs. Only one checked move held, and the human-move model says it was hard to find.
The capture looks natural to the human-move model, but the recapture takes back a bigger piece. Count a trade all the way to its last capture.
This capture starts a trade where the recapture takes back more. One other checked move held, and the human-move model says it was hard to find. Count it all the way through.
Fork: a lone attacker against a handful of targets. The human-move model calls it the natural pick, and the engine puts it at the top. Easy and right together.
A fork, with a lone attacker hitting more than one thing. The human-move model figured on this move. The engine has it down as strong, with one move above it.
This lets one of their pieces fork several targets. Just one checked move held, and the human-move model says it was a tricky one to find. That defense is worth learning.
A fork was sitting there, one piece able to hit several targets. The human-move model calls the move played the natural pick, and the fork goes by. Forcing moves first.
Of the checked moves, only a fork held, one piece on several targets. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was a hard find. Track down the piece that does it.
A pin against the king, and the engine's top move. With its king behind it, the pinned piece cannot get off that line. The human-move model calls it the natural pick. Easy and right together.
That piece is pinned, with its king behind, and chained down. The human-move model calls it natural, and the engine's call on it is strong, with one move above it.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and it gives the other side a pin against the king. A piece pinned like that cannot leave its line.
The other side now gets to pin a piece in front of its king. Only one checked move held up, and by the human-move model it was hard to spot. Learn why it holds.
A pin against the king was the better move, nailing a piece to its line. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and the pin goes unused.
A pin against the king was the only checked move that held. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was a hard one to spot. Hard defenses are still worth learning.
Skewer, and the engine's first choice. Front piece hit, front piece moves, back piece falls. Both the human-move model and the checked moves say it was tough to find.
A skewer: the front piece gets hit, and the piece behind it is open once the front one moves. The human-move model rates it an unusual pick. Strong, says the engine, all the same.
A skewer: two pieces on a line, and the attack goes through the first to the second. The human-move model calls it natural, and the engine puts it at the top. Right on.
Skewer. Two pieces, one line, and the back one is the prize. The human-move model calls it natural, and the engine weighs it in as strong, though one move sits above it.
Two pieces stand in a row, ready for a skewer by the other side. A single checked move held, and the human-move model has it down as hard to dig up. That move is worth some study.
A skewer was in the better move: go at the front piece, and its partner behind is lost. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and the skewer stays on the board.
A skewer was in the only checked move that held. It was missed, and by the human-move model it was a hard thing to see. Go back until you can see it.
The guard goes first: this takes the defender, and what it held up is left with no help. The engine's top move, and by the human-move model a tricky one to find.
The target is the guard. Once it is gone, nothing protects what it covered. The human-move model rates the move unusual, and the engine has it down as strong.
Take the defender, and what it guarded has no help. Natural to the human-move model, and first on the engine's list. No reason to wait.
Off comes the defender, and what it guarded is now unguarded. Natural, as the human-move model sees it. The engine calls it strong; one move rates a bit higher.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, but now a defender can be knocked out, and what it guards would have no help.
A defender can now be knocked out by the other side. Just one checked move held, and it was not the one played. The human-move model says it was a hard find.
The better move knocked out a defender and left what it guarded bare. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and the defender stays at work.
The one checked move that held took a defender. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was hard to see. Learn that defense.
Its own pieces have the king boxed in at the back, and this move goes after that. The engine's top move, and by the human-move model a hard one to spot. Strong.
Its own pieces trap the king on the back row, and this move goes right at that. The human-move model rates it unusual; the engine's call on it is strong.
Back-row mate is the target: the king has no air, walled in by its own men. It is the human-move model's natural pick and the engine's first choice.
The king is boxed in on its back row, and this move aims there. The human-move model counts it as a natural pick. Strong, says the engine, though it likes another move a bit more.
The big thing is the pawn and its walk to the last row. This is the engine's top move, and the human-move model says it was a hard thing to see. That pawn could settle the game.
Simple point: this pawn is heading for promotion. Not a move the human-move model expects, but the engine marks it strong.
The pawn heads for the last row and promotion. The human-move model calls it natural; the engine likes it best of all. Keep that pawn moving.
This is about the pawn, and how close it is to promotion. The human-move model expects this one. By the engine's count it is strong, just not first.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and it gives one of their pawns a clear walk toward the last row. That pawn needs stopping early.
Now a pawn of theirs can walk to promotion. Just one checked move held, and the human-move model says it was a tricky one to find. Spend some time on that defense.
The better move pushed a pawn toward the last row. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and the pawn stays put. Count the pawn's steps first.
Of the checked moves, only a pawn push toward promotion held. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was a hard find.
The front piece clears out, and a discovered attack lands. The engine's top move, and by the human-move model a hard one to spot. Strong.
Shift the front piece, and the piece behind it gets into the fight, a discovered attack. The human-move model rates it unusual, and the engine puts it in the strong column.
A discovered attack: the blocker clears out and the back piece attacks. The human-move model expects it, and the engine rates nothing above it.
The front piece clears the way for the one behind it, which is what a discovered attack means. The human-move model calls it natural; the engine has it down as strong, with one move above it.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and it lets one of their front pieces step aside for an attack from behind.
This lets the other side uncover an attack from behind a front piece. Just one checked move held, and the human-move model says it was hard to see.
Discovered attack was the better move: front piece aside, back piece in. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and that attack stays hidden.
Of the checked moves, only a discovered attack held. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was a hard thing to see.
Double attack, and the engine's top move. The human-move model and the checked moves say it was a tricky one to find. Strong.
Double attack. Maybe no reply saves both. The human-move model rates it an unusual pick, and the engine's call on it is strong.
A double attack, and both targets need an answer. The human-move model calls it natural, and the engine puts it at the top.
Double attack. Both targets are hit, and the defense may have to give one up. For the human-move model, this is a natural pick. The engine has it as strong, a step below its top choice.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and it hands the other side a double attack. A reply has to cover both.
The other side gets to hit two things with one piece. Just one checked move held, and it was missed. Few players would spot it, by the human-move model's count.
Two attacks at once was the better move. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and the double attack never happens.
Of the checked moves, only a double attack held. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was hard to see.
Deflection: the defender is hauled off, and what it covered is bare. The engine's top move, and by the human-move model a hard find. Strong.
A defender gets dragged off what it protects. The human-move model rates that unusual, and the engine marks it strong.
Haul the defender off, and nobody covers what it covered. Natural to the human-move model, and first on the engine's list.
A deflection: a guard is hauled away, and its post sits empty. A predictable pick for the human-move model. Strong by the engine, with one move ranked ahead.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and now the other side can drag a defender off its job. That job would be left undone.
A defender can now be dragged away by the other side. Only one checked move held up, and by the human-move model it was hard to spot.
The better move dragged a defender off its job. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and that defender keeps working.
The one checked move that held was a deflection, dragging a defender away. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was a hard one to spot.
This move collects a piece that had no protection. The engine's top move, and the human-move model says it was a hard thing to see. Spotted, and taken.
A loose piece, and it is collected. The human-move model calls it unusual; the engine calls it strong.
That piece was unprotected, and the move picks it up. It is the human-move model's natural pick and the engine's first choice. That is all there is to it.
That piece was loose, so the move collects it. Natural, as the human-move model sees it. The engine weighs it in as strong, though one move sits above it.
The better move picked up a piece with no guard. The human-move model calls the move played natural, and the loose piece stays put. Loose pieces first.
The one checked move that held took a piece with no guard. It was missed, and the human-move model says it was hard to notice. Loose pieces are the first thing to spot.
The human-move model calls this a natural pick, and a piece is left loose for the other side to pick up. Natural, and still a mistake.
A piece is left loose, so the other side may scoop it up. Just one checked move held, and the human-move model says it was hard to see. Learn it.
Development: a minor piece leaves home and starts pulling weight. The human-move model and the checked moves say it was a hard move to find. The obvious move is not always the developing one.
Development: a minor piece is out. The human-move model rates it an unusual pick, and the engine has it down as strong.
A minor piece comes out and starts working. The human-move model calls it natural; the engine likes it best of all. Plain and right.
Development: a minor piece leaves home and starts pulling weight. The human-move model counts it as a natural pick. The engine calls it strong; one move rates a bit higher.
The rook gets a clear road: an open file. The human-move model and the checked moves both point to a tricky one to find. Now use that road.
The rook gets a file with nothing on it but itself. The human-move model rates it unusual, and the engine's call on it is strong.
Rook on the open file, clear road ahead. The human-move model expects it, and the engine rates nothing above it.
Plain fact: this rook now runs a pawnless file. For the human-move model, this is a natural pick. Strong, says the engine, though it likes another move a bit more.
Half-open, that file: its own pawns gone, an enemy pawn still sitting there to aim at. Both the human-move model and the checked moves say it was tough to find.
